title: Swing District Voters Oppose Data Center Expansion, NBC Poll Shows
dek: An NBC News Decision Desk Poll conducted August 20 through September 1 found 69% of voters in swing districts oppose AI data center construction in their local areas. The opposition cuts across party lines, with 57% of Republicans, 81% of Democrats, and 71% of independents against local data center development.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: 69% of voters in swing districts critical to 2026 House control oppose AI data center construction locally, per NBC News Decision Desk Poll conducted August 20 through September 1.
bottom_line: The NBC polling captures voter sentiment in districts that will determine House control before the November 2026 midterms, at a moment when local moratoriums and state regulation are already limiting data center expansion and when Republican incumbents are shifting positions. Whether the unified opposition holds through the general election will test whether Trump's pro-expansion stance can move opinion or whether elected officials in swing races continue retreating from data center support.
body: Voters across swing districts critical to 2026 House control broadly oppose artificial intelligence data center construction in their communities, according to NBC News Decision Desk polling conducted August 20 through September 1. The finding creates political tension as President Trump advocates for rapid data center expansion while elected officials in contested races navigate constituent opposition.

The NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 69% of respondents in swing districts oppose construction of AI data centers in their local area, with 45% saying they "strongly oppose" the idea. The opposition spans party lines: 57% of Republican voters oppose data centers in their communities versus 43% in favor, per the same polling. Among Democrats, 81% oppose data centers being built locally, and 71% of independents oppose them.

NBC News surveyed voters along Interstate 80 from Nebraska to New Jersey, a region that includes eight swing districts key to determining House control and two marquee Senate races. In Buchanan County, Iowa, which favored Trump 63% to 35% in 2024, county supervisors approved a temporary moratorium banning data centers from the county. Republican county supervisor Dawn Vogel, who voted for the moratorium, stated she "hasn't talked to a single voter at home who wants data centers."

Politicians in contested races are responding to constituent concerns. Rep. Marcy Kaptur, a 22-term Democrat from Ohio, is using the data center issue against Republican rival Derek Merrin, who cast a 2017 vote in the state Legislature that helped extend tax breaks to companies that build data centers in Ohio. Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican seeking to hold his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, introduced legislation in July requiring utility companies to charge large-scale data center operators enough to cover increased electricity and water use costs. Husted was previously a full-throated advocate for data centers when he served as Ohio's lieutenant governor, according to NBC News. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat on the ballot in November, signed a new batch of data center regulations in August after having encouraged companies to locate data centers in his state.

At the federal level, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) have proposed a data center moratorium covering the entire country. Trump wrote on Truth Social in late August: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign."

Support for data centers comes from national and local labor unions involved in data center construction and maintenance, who tout them as a source of jobs and high rates of pay. A data center worker in Ohio, speaking anonymously per NBC News, stated he can make as much as $5,000 in a week including overtime at a relatively low-level union position. The same worker said he was warned by friends about negative effects like water overuse and unusual sounds but "didn't see any of the things" he was told about at his workplace, and noted the industry is "helping a lot of people with a lot of work going on." Democratic voter Tamara Clark, 49, a healthcare industry worker in Ohio, raised concerns that data centers drive utility costs up for citizens in the area, stating: "I don't feel like the rich should continuously get rich while we have to grovel for what we need in our everyday necessities."
